analysis.one_liner: Makes employers legally liable for workplace harassment by bosses and lead workers who direct employees' daily work.
analysis.headline: The Senate labor committee never acted on the bill: introduced in October 2017 with five Democratic cosponsors, it received no hearing and no vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2013 Supreme Court ruling, Vance v. Ball State University, narrowed who counts as a 'supervisor' in harassment cases, so employers can escape liability when a harasser can direct a worker's day-to-day duties but cannot formally hire, fire, or demote them. This bill would reverse that by statute across major federal anti-discrimination laws, including the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the ADA, and the Congressional Accountability Act. Employers would be liable if the harasser could direct the victim's daily work or recommend job actions against them, or if the employer's own negligence let the hostile environment arise or continue.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are harassed by shift leads, foremen, or other low-level supervisors who control their daily work but lack formal power to hire or fire. The bill's findings single out low-wage workers in restaurants, retail, health care, housekeeping, and personal care, where such lead workers are common, as well as federal employees, congressional employees, and workers with disabilities and older workers covered by the other statutes.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-Vance liability standard: employers are liable when the harasser could direct the victim's daily work activities or recommend tangible employment actions, or when employer negligence caused the hostile environment [S2][S3].

Applies the standard across ten statutes, including Title VII, the ADEA, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, and the Congressional Accountability Act, so it covers private, federal, and congressional workplaces [S3].

The bill's own findings document the stakes: in the restaurant industry, two-thirds of women reported sexual harassment from management, and harassment by lead workers is concentrated in low-wage industries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face more lawsuits and greater liability when lead workers or negligent management practices create hostile work environments. The burden falls heaviest on low-wage service industries, and employers would also carry litigation and settlement costs in federal workplaces and congressional offices.

drawbacks.text: Section 12 explicitly preserves all existing employer defenses, so the bill leaves the Faragher/Ellerth affirmative defense intact; it expands only who counts as a supervisor, not the full range of employer liability [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection is cost: holding employers automatically liable for the conduct of any worker who directs daily duties would raise litigation exposure, and businesses argued after Vance that the Court's rule drew a workable line between lead workers and true supervisors. Small operators in tight-margin industries would bear real compliance and insurance costs.

The bill applies to all claims pending on or after enactment, applying a new liability standard retroactively to existing disputes, which employers could argue upends expectations in ongoing cases [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers the benefit is direct and concrete: under Vance, a harassed employee whose tormentor schedules her shifts but cannot formally fire her may have no vicarious-liability claim at all, and the bill's findings document that this situation is common precisely in low-wage industries with the least workplace power. The costs are real but the ordinary costs of enforcing anti-discrimination law: more suits, more settlements, more pressure on employers to police lead workers. The bill is also modestly designed, keeping the existing affirmative defense for employers who exercise reasonable care. The main honest caveat is that automatic liability for lead workers could push some small employers toward rigid management structures or higher insurance costs without guaranteeing less harassment.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in October 2017, and the committee never held a hearing or vote; the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2019 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on October 26, 2017, joined by Democratic Sens. Durbin, Markey, Blumenthal, and Leahy [S1][S3].

It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, which was the last action of record; no hearing, markup, or vote followed in the remainder of the 115th Congress [S5][S1].
The House saw a companion effort in this era (the Fair Employment Protection Act has been introduced in prior Congresses), but this Senate bill never advanced past referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced liability for harassment by lead workers, especially large low-wage service businesses, and congressional employing offices, all of whom avoid the stricter standard; harassed workers whose harassers direct their daily work but cannot formally hire or fire them remain without the remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, especially large low-wage service chains

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its advocacy in the Senate.

against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral in October 2017.

against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.role: Opponents of restoring the pre-Vance liability standard
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against legislation overturning Vance v. Ball State University, arguing it would expand employer litigation exposure; their opposition kept the bill off the committee agenda.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Senate Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Restaurants and other low-wage service employers (retail, health care, housekeeping, personal care)
industries.note: These industries have the most lead workers who direct daily duties without formal hiring power, and the bill's findings document pervasive harassment in them. The bill would make their employers liable for such harassment, creating direct incentive to police it.

Would face vicarious liability for harassment by any worker authorized to direct daily work or recommend job actions, plus liability where employer negligence let a hostile environment persist, increasing litigation and settlement exposure.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and congressional employing offices
industries.note: The bill applies the same liability standard to federal workplaces and to Congress itself through the Congressional Accountability Act, meaning members' offices and agencies could be sued under the stricter standard.

industries.industry: Employment defense bar and employment practices insurers
industries.note: More hostile-environment claims would increase demand for defense litigation and employment practices liability coverage, costs ultimately passed to employers and workers.
